elements.text: Why teams put Cloudflare in front

Every request to a site on Cloudflare hits the nearest data center first, where it is checked against the WAF, served from cache when possible, and only then forwarded to the origin over a warm connection. That is what turns a single server into something that survives a launch day.

elements.text: Also on the network
WAF, bot management, rate limiting, load balancing, Argo smart routing, Spectrum for TCP and UDP, Zero Trust access and gateway, and Cloudflare Tunnel for origins with no public address.
Workers
Serverless code on the edge

Workers run your code in V8 isolates at every Cloudflare location. There is no cold start you can measure, no region to pick, and no container to build. Deploy with wrangler and the code is live everywhere in seconds.

Bindings connect a Worker to the rest of the platform: KV for eventually consistent config, Durable Objects for coordination and state, D1 for SQL, Queues for background work, and R2 for objects. Each binding is a variable on the env object; there is no SDK to configure.
R2 Storage
Object storage without egress fees

R2 stores objects behind an S3-compatible API, so existing tools, SDKs, and backup jobs work with a change of endpoint. The difference is the bill: reading data out to the internet costs nothing, which changes what is worth storing at the edge.

Buckets can be public, served through a custom domain with the CDN in front, or private and reached only from a Worker binding. Multipart uploads, presigned URLs, lifecycle rules, and event notifications to Queues are all supported.

children.text:
$ wrangler r2 bucket create media
$ wrangler r2 object put media/hero.png --file ./hero.png
$ wrangler r2 object get media/hero.png

elements.text: DNS
Authoritative DNS that answers in milliseconds

Cloudflare DNS is anycast from every data center, so a resolver anywhere reaches the nearest copy of your zone. Changes propagate globally in seconds rather than the hours a traditional TTL would suggest, and DNSSEC signing is one toggle.
Records can be proxied, which routes traffic through the CDN and WAF, or DNS-only, which publishes the origin address directly. Import a zone file, use the API, or manage records with Terraform.

children.text:
$ dig +short example.com A
104.16.132.229
104.16.133.229
$ dig +short example.com NS
ada.ns.cloudflare.com.
rob.ns.cloudflare.com.

What is DNS?
The Domain Name System turns names people can remember into addresses machines can route.

When you type a domain into a browser, the operating system asks a recursive resolver for the address. The resolver walks the hierarchy: the root servers point to the .com servers, which point to the authoritative name servers for the domain, which return the record. Each answer is cached for the record's TTL so the next lookup is local.

Record types carry different facts. A and AAAA hold IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, CNAME aliases one name to another, MX names the mail servers, TXT holds verification strings and policies such as SPF, and NS delegates a zone.

DNS was designed without authentication. DNSSEC adds signatures so a resolver can verify a record came from the zone owner, and DNS over HTTPS or TLS encrypts the query between the client and its resolver so the network in between cannot read or alter it.

/learning/what-is-a-cdn.title: What is a CDN? · Cloudflare Learning

elements.text: What is a CDN?
A content delivery network keeps copies of your content close to the people who ask for it.

A CDN is a set of servers spread across many locations. When a request arrives it is routed to the nearest one, which serves the response from cache if it has a fresh copy and otherwise fetches it from the origin, stores it, and returns it. The origin sees one request instead of thousands.

Caching is governed by HTTP headers. Cache-Control decides how long a response may be reused, ETag and Last-Modified let the edge revalidate cheaply, and Vary tells it which request headers change the answer. Dynamic pages still benefit: the TLS handshake and the TCP connection happen at the edge, and the round trip to the origin runs over a warm, tuned connection.
Beyond speed, sitting in front of the origin makes a CDN the natural place to absorb attacks, terminate TLS, and apply a firewall. The origin's address never needs to be public.
What is TLS?
Transport Layer Security encrypts and authenticates the connection between a client and a server.

TLS is the protocol behind the padlock. The client and server perform a handshake: they agree on a cipher suite, the server presents a certificate signed by a certificate authority the client trusts, and the two derive session keys through an ephemeral key exchange. Everything after that is encrypted and integrity-checked.

TLS 1.3, standardized in 2018, cut the handshake to one round trip, removed obsolete ciphers, and encrypts more of the handshake itself. Session resumption and 0-RTT let returning clients skip most of the work.

A certificate binds a domain name to a public key. Universal SSL on Cloudflare issues and renews one automatically for every proxied domain; the edge terminates TLS from the visitor and opens a separate encrypted connection to the origin.

/blog/workers-platform-2026.title: The Workers platform in 2026: what changed and what is next · Cloudflare Blog

elements.text: Developer platform
The Workers platform in 2026: what changed and what is next
Ines Marchetti · 2026-04-08

This year's Developer Week shipped three things we have been asked for since Workers launched: native Python with a real package ecosystem, Durable Objects with SQLite storage and point-in-time recovery, and a container runtime for the jobs that do not fit in an isolate.

The container runtime is the one that surprised people. A Worker can now start a container next to itself, hand it a request, and stream back the response, all inside the same deployment. Video transcoding, headless browsers, and language toolchains that expect a filesystem finally have a home on the platform without leaving it.

Next up is the workflow engine, which is in open beta. A workflow is a Worker whose steps are durable: if a step fails or the process is evicted, it resumes from the last completed step with the same inputs. We use it internally for every multi-stage migration.

/blog/post-quantum-by-default.title: Post-quantum key agreement is now the default for every proxied site · Cloudflare Blog

elements.text: Security
Post-quantum key agreement is now the default for every proxied site
Dmitri Sokolov · 2026-02-17

As of this week, every TLS 1.3 handshake to a Cloudflare-proxied site negotiates a hybrid key agreement that combines X25519 with ML-KEM. If the browser supports it, and every major browser now does, the session keys cannot be recovered by a future quantum computer that recorded the traffic today.

The change is invisible to site owners. The certificate chain is unchanged; only the ephemeral key exchange is affected, so there is nothing to renew or reconfigure. Origins that speak TLS to us are also covered when the connection is set to Full (strict).

We measured a median of one extra kilobyte in the ClientHello and no measurable change in handshake latency once the packet fits in the initial congestion window. Over 60 percent of human traffic on our network was already post-quantum protected before the default flipped.

/blog/outage-2026-03-04-postmortem.title: Postmortem: DNS resolution errors on March 4, 2026 · Cloudflare Blog

elements.text: Incident review
Postmortem: DNS resolution errors on March 4, 2026
Hannah Okafor · 2026-03-06

For 23 minutes on March 4, between 14:11 and 14:34 UTC, some authoritative DNS queries for zones on Cloudflare returned SERVFAIL. About 4 percent of queries in that window were affected, concentrated in two European locations.

Root cause: a configuration push that changed the zone database sharding rolled out to two data centers whose local cache still held the previous shard map. Queries that hashed to a moved shard could not find their zone. The rollout was automatically halted when error rates crossed the threshold, and the two locations were drained while the caches refreshed.

What we changed: a shard map change now invalidates the local cache in the same transaction, and the canary stage of the rollout waits for a full cache refresh before proceeding. We are sorry for the disruption; the Status page carries the full timeline.

elements.text: Deploy your first Worker
From an empty directory to a URL that answers, in five commands.
1. Install wrangler with npm and log in. The login opens the dashboard in a browser and stores an API token locally.
2. Create a project. The template writes a src/index.ts with a fetch handler and a wrangler.toml naming the Worker.
3. Run it locally with wrangler dev, which emulates the runtime and every binding on your machine, then deploy. The output prints a workers.dev URL that is live everywhere immediately.

children.text:
$ npm install -g wrangler
$ wrangler login
$ npm create cloudflare@latest hello-worker
$ cd hello-worker && wrangler dev
$ wrangler deploy
Deployed hello-worker to https://hello-worker.example.workers.dev

/docs/r2-bucket-basics.title: R2 buckets from a Worker · Cloudflare Docs

elements.text: R2 buckets from a Worker
Bind a bucket, then read and write objects with the env binding.
1. Create the bucket, then declare a binding in wrangler.toml. The binding name becomes a property on env inside the Worker.
2. The binding exposes get, put, delete, list, and head. Objects carry HTTP metadata, so a Worker can serve them directly with the right content type.
3. For public buckets, connect a custom domain in the dashboard and the CDN serves objects with caching and no Worker at all.
